- VC-65: FAIL (suggestion) — The comment asserts that, under each listed dialect (None, sqlite, and mysql for 'c\nSELECT n FROM widgets'), the statement does not parse and so is not read-shaped. [tests/unit/test_safety_limits.py:670]

  <details><summary>Evidence</summary>

  The comment at tests/unit/test_safety_limits.py:670-673 says that under None, sqlite and mysql the statement 'does not parse, so it is not read-shaped'. The code does not classify by parsing. RunSqlTool.execute calls is_read_shaped(args.sql, self.dialect) (src/sqllens/agent/tools/run_sql.py:77). is_read_shaped (src/sqllens/safety/readonly.py:167-175) is `first_sql_keyword(sql, dialect) in _READ_SHAPED_KEYWORDS`. first_sql_keyword (readonly.py:124-164) only runs resolved.tokenize(sql) and looks at the first token. A TokenError gives '' and a parse is never attempted. For the mysql row 'c\nSELECT n FROM widgets', the tokenizer accepts the input. Its first token `c` is TokenType.VAR (readonly.py:156-157), so first_sql_keyword returns 'C'. 'C' is not in _READ_SHAPED_KEYWORDS, which is why the statement is not read-shaped. That is the falsifying input from verify_hint: a successful tokenization whose first keyword is not a read keyword, and no parse failure involved. For the None and sqlite rows, '# c' tokenizes as TokenType.HASH (sqlglot/tokens.py:156). That is not a VAR or a word, so first_sql_keyword returns '' by the same mechanism. The statements are probably also unparseable (sqlglot parser.py:2311-2312 raises on leftover tokens), but parse failure is not what makes them non-read-shaped. A parseable statement starting with a non-read keyword is non-read-shaped too, and an unparseable one starting with SELECT would be read-shaped. The causal claim in the comment is therefore wrong, and a reader would take the wrong mechanism from it. The test's assertions are unaffected. The rejections line concerns the pragma_/mysql.func row in test_safety.py and does not cover this comment.

  </details>
